slides.heading: Sum Bsts
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Binary Search Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Sum Bsts, a hard binary search trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Sum the values of every node that roots a valid BST subtree containing at least 3 nodes.
Post-order collecting (isBst, size, min, max, sum).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Sum the values of every node that roots a valid BST subtree containing at least 3 nodes. Post-order collecting (isBst, size, min, max, sum).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Post-order lets each node know whether both children are BSTs, their sizes, sums and value ranges.
slides.narration: Post-order lets each node know whether both children are BSTs, their sizes, sums and value ranges.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: For each node validate subtree, then sum → O(n²)
Single post-order pass returning (isBst, size, min, max, sum) → O(n)
slides.narration: Validating each subtree separately is quadratic. One post-order pass that returns validity, size, min, max and sum lets every node decide in constant time.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Return validity, size, sum, min and max from each subtree
3. Add sums of valid BSTs with three or more nodes
slides.narration: Step by step. First, return validity, size, sum, min and max from each subtree. Second, combine at the parent. Third, add sums of valid BSTs with three or more nodes.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Post-order: return BST info upward
slides.narration: Each node returns whether its subtree is a BST, its size, min, max and sum, computed from its children.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Subtree at 7 is a BST of size 3 → 22
slides.narration: The subtree rooted at seven, with six and nine, is a BST with three nodes, sum twenty-two.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Subtree at 5 is a bigger BST → 30
slides.narration: At five, the left max is three and the right min is six, so it's a BST of five nodes summing to thirty. That replaces the twenty-two we counted inside it.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Other subtrees fail → answer 30
slides.narration: Two has a right child of one, which breaks the BST rule, so the root fails too. The answer is thirty.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: Info recurses on both children, decides BST status from their max and min, and when the subtree is a BST of size three or more adds its sum, subtracting children already counted. It returns the tuple.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is O of h.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
slides.narration: Only subtrees with at least three nodes count, and a larger valid BST replaces the contributions of the smaller ones inside it.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: State the tuple you return from each call clearly; it's the whole trick.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Post-order lets each node know whether both children are BSTs, their sizes, sums and value ranges.
slides.narration: To recap Sum Bsts: Post-order lets each node know whether both children are BSTs, their sizes, sums and value ranges. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
